name: Memory conformity
statement: When two people who saw the same event discuss it, each takes details from the other's account and later reports them as things they saw themselves.
meaning: The claim is about a specific channel for memory error: another person who was there. Classic misinformation studies deliver the false detail through a leading question or a written narrative, and the implied author is an experimenter who presumably knows the answer. A co-witness is different. The source is a peer, present in the room, no better placed than the listener, and the listener has every reason to treat their memory as fallible. Two laboratory traditions test whether the error travels anyway. In the social contagion paradigm a confederate slips items that were never there into a joint recall session. In the co-witness paradigms the two people watch versions of the same film that differ in a handful of details, believe they watched the same thing, discuss it, and are then tested alone. Both ask the same question: does the other person's report change what this person later says they remember. The forensic interest is that real witnesses talk. Where the effect matters is the gap between what a statement claims to be, an independent account, and what it may be, a version of somebody else's.

origin.who: Daniel B. Wright, Gail Self and Chris Justice
origin.note: The name comes from the title of their two experiments on post-event information delivered by another person. Roediger, Meade and Bergman named the same phenomenon the social contagion of memory a year later, working from Asch rather than from eyewitness research, and the two literatures ran in parallel for years. The paper the forensic field is built on is Gabbert, Memon and Allan's dyad procedure of 2003.

evidence: Roediger, Meade and Bergman ran 24 Washington University undergraduates through six household scenes, each shown for 15 or 60 seconds and containing an average of 23.8 objects. A confederate posing as a second participant took turns recalling six items per scene, and for three of the six scenes slipped in one item that had not been there. Tested alone afterwards, with accuracy stressed, participants recalled the suggested items on 22% of occasions against 6% for the same items when they had not been suggested, F(1, 22) = 23.87, p < .01. Items a pilot group had listed as expected in that scene, such as a toaster in a kitchen, travelled better than unexpected ones such as oven mitts, 33% against 11%. The shorter viewing time produced the larger effect, 22% against 10%. Most of the false recall was not experienced as recollection. Falsely recalled contagion items drew a know judgement 17% of the time and a remember judgement 5% of the time. Meade and Roediger took the paradigm through four experiments. Warning 37 participants between the joint and the individual test that the other person had made mistakes cut the contagion effect from .30 to .11, and it survived the warning, t(17) = 2.15. The warning also cost accuracy: correct items the confederate had recalled were later recalled .37 of the time under warning against .47 without it. Suggesting an item four times in written protocols produced a larger effect than suggesting it once, .32 against .09, F(2, 28) = 21.56. Gabbert, Memon and Allan moved the design to pairs who each watched a different video of the same staged crime and believed they had watched the same one. Their abstract reports that 71% of the witnesses who discussed the event went on to recall items they could only have got from the discussion. Susceptibility did not differ between adults aged 18 to 30 and adults aged 60 to 80. Gabbert, Memon and Wright then taped and transcribed the discussions of 64 participants shown four pairs of complex pictures differing in two details each. Whoever mentioned a contested item first usually won. First mentioners reported their own version at test 79% of the time; recipients managed 32%, and reported the partner's version instead 35% of the time. A second experiment with 58 participants and a staged burglary sorted the details by type. Added details, mentioned by a partner but absent from one's own film, were the most contagious at 45%, ahead of contradicted details at 29% and details one had seen but the partner omitted at 10%. The channel matters as much as the content. Gabbert, Memon, Allan and Wright gave young and older adults four items of misinformation about a filmed crime. It arrived either in conversation with a confederate or embedded in a written narrative they were asked to read. Their abstract reports that the socially delivered version misled more, in both age groups. Witnesses often are not alone. Paterson and Kemp screened 773 Australian psychology undergraduates. Three quarters had witnessed a serious event, most often a physical assault, and 86% of those reported at least one other witness present, a mean of 6.77 and a median of 3. Of the 60 who completed a follow-up questionnaire about a specific event, 86% had discussed it with a co-witness and 63% had spoken about it immediately.

replication.headline: A ten-country replication of the co-witness procedure found the effect in every sample, with a pooled Hedges' g of 1.70, and located almost all of it in the cases where the listener let the other account stand.
replication.detail: Ito and 18 co-authors repeated Garry, French, Kinzett and Mori's version of Mori's MORI technique in Brazil, Canada, Colombia, India, Japan, Malaysia, Poland, Portugal, Turkey and the United Kingdom, N = 486, with the second batch of five samples preregistered. Pairs sat side by side wearing filtered glasses and watched what they believed was one film, answered questions together in a way that forced the differences into the open, then took a recognition test alone. Recognition accuracy on discussed items fell below accuracy on non-discussed items in all ten samples, all ps < .001, F(1, 405) = 687.57 for the discussion factor with partial eta squared of .63. Pooling the ten new samples gave g = 1.70, 95% CI [1.40, 1.99], Z = 11.17, and adding Garry and colleagues' New Zealand sample gave g = 1.67, 95% CI [1.40, 1.94], Z = 12.19. The authors put the New Zealand estimate at g = 1.46, 95% CI [0.85, 2.07]. The size of the effect varied, from a 34-point accuracy gap in Colombia to 64 points in Japan, and the interaction with country was reliable, F(9, 405) = 2.46, p = .010. The moderator that explains it is not culture but whether the listener pushed back. Across the ten samples 708 discussed items went undisputed and 58 were disputed. Where the co-witness's answer went unchallenged, the listener later gave that wrong answer in 626 of 708 cases, or 88.4%. Where it had been challenged, one case in 58 went wrong. Disputes were not spread evenly: 30 of the 58 came from the Canadian sample and 10 from the Colombian, four samples recorded none at all, and Japan was one of them. Ito and colleagues point out that this does not fit a collectivism story, because Colombia is the most collectivist of the ten countries on Hofstede's index and Canada among the most individualist. The pattern repeats online. Kękuś, Szpitalak, Polczyk and Barzykowski ran 36 Polish pairs over a video call. Among the 66 participants who received any misinformation, accuracy was .74 on non-discussed items and .38 on discussed ones, F(1, 65) = 54.06, Hedges' g = 1.17, 95% CI [0.68, 1.69]. Among the 36 who disputed something at least once, accuracy on disputed items was .84 against .17 on undisputed ones.

limits: This entry covers discussion between adults who witnessed the same event. It does not cover children's suggestibility or interrogative suggestibility, which the suggestibility entry carries, nor implanted childhood events and the word-list paradigm, which the false memory entry carries, nor collaborative recall as a way of improving accuracy. The search ran across Crossref, OpenAlex, PubMed, PMC, Semantic Scholar, institutional repositories and the open web. Several papers were not obtained. Gabbert, Memon and Allan (2003) is paywalled and has no repository copy, so the 71% and the age comparison are quoted from the abstract at Crossref and the per-item rate is not given here. Garry, French, Kinzett and Mori (2008) is paywalled on the same terms, and the New Zealand effect size attributed to it is Ito and colleagues' recomputation of it inside their own meta-analysis rather than a figure printed in the 2008 paper. Wright, Self and Justice (2000) is paywalled and is cited here only for the name and for what its abstract says. Wright, Memon, Skagerberg and Gabbert's 2009 review could not be fetched and nothing is claimed from it. The Ito figures were read from the author accepted manuscript in the Warwick repository, not the version of record. That manuscript disagrees with itself. Its results section gives g = 1.67, 95% CI [1.40, 1.94] with the New Zealand sample and g = 1.70, 95% CI [1.40, 1.99] without it. Its discussion pairs the 1.70 with the 1.94 interval. Whether the published version fixes this was not checked. No meta-analysis of the memory conformity literature as a whole was located; the pooled figure quoted here covers eleven runs of one procedure. The paradigms also bound what they show. The details at stake are peripheral, a red cap or a green car, and the co-witness is usually a stranger met minutes earlier in a psychology department. Nothing here establishes how long a conformed detail lasts, whether it survives a formal police interview, or what happens when the disputed fact is who committed the crime.
misreadings: The 71% is treated as the rate at which discussion corrupts memory. It is a headcount, not an item rate: 71% of the witnesses who discussed the event reported at least one detail they could only have heard from the other person. The number that describes items is Ito and colleagues' 88.4%, and it is conditional. It applies to the 708 cases in which the listener let the other account stand, and where the listener argued the figure was one case in 58. Conformity read as automatic misses the condition attached to it. A second reading takes the effect as proof that memory itself has changed. Some of it is people going along with the room. Garry and colleagues report in their abstract that agreeing during the discussion and reverting to one's own answer at test was the minority pattern. That is what pure compliance looks like. Most agreement, they say, happened because the other answer seemed right. Roediger and colleagues' remember and know judgements point the same way from the other side. Falsely recalled suggested items drew a know judgement 17% of the time against a remember judgement 5% of the time. The items came back as things the person was confident about rather than things they could picture. Warnings are read as a fix. Meade and Roediger warned participants that the other person had made errors, and the effect fell from .30 to .11 without disappearing. The same warning cut recall of the correct items the confederate had contributed from .47 to .37. Telling a witness to distrust a co-witness costs the accurate information along with the inaccurate. The influence is also read as purely destructive. Roediger and colleagues noted that where their confederate recalled all six items correctly, participants later recalled 43% of those items against 26% for items neither person had mentioned, and flagged the comparison as tentative because it was not counterbalanced. Updating a memory from someone who saw the same thing is usually a good bet, and the false memories are the price. The last misreading is procedural. Memory conformity is not a claim that eyewitnesses are unreliable; it is a claim about what happens to independence when they talk. Paterson and Kemp's respondents talked 86% of the time.

Paywalled; the abstract was read at Crossref and is the source for the name and for the description of the two experiments.

Roediger, H. L., Meade, M. L., & Bergman, E. T. (2001). Social contagion of memory. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 8(2), 365-371. Read in full from the publisher's PDF; source for every figure in the contagion paragraph.
Meade, M. L., & Roediger, H. L. (2002). Explorations in the social contagion of memory. Memory & Cognition, 30(7), 995-1009. Read in full; source for the warning and repetition results.

Gabbert, F., Memon, A., & Allan, K. (2003). Memory conformity: Can eyewitnesses influence each other's memories for an event? Applied Cognitive Psychology, 17(5), 533-543. Paywalled with no repository copy; the 71% and the age comparison are taken from the abstract at Crossref.

Gabbert, F., Memon, A., Allan, K., & Wright, D. B. (2004). Say it to my face: Examining the effects of socially encountered misinformation. Legal and Criminological Psychology, 9(2), 215-227. Abstract read at Crossref; cited for the finding that misinformation from a person misled more than the same misinformation in a written narrative, in both younger and older adults.

Gabbert, F., Memon, A., & Wright, D. B. (2006). Memory conformity: Disentangling the steps toward influence during a discussion. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 13(3), 480-485. Read in full; source for the first-mention figures and the added, contradicted and omitted comparison.

Paywalled; the abstract was read at Crossref and is the source for the compliance-versus-acceptance claim. The effect size attributed to this study comes from Ito and colleagues' meta-analysis, not from this paper.
